history.heading: Pre-Columbian cultures
paragraphs: Colombia's territory was home to many indigenous societies, including the Muisca in the Andean highlands, renowned goldsmiths whose ritual of covering a chief in gold dust inspired the legend of El Dorado, the Tairona in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, who built Ciudad Perdida (the Lost City), and the San Agustín culture, known for monumental stone statues.

history.heading: Spanish colony
paragraphs: Spanish explorers arrived in 1499, and Cartagena de Indias, founded in 1533, became a major port and fortress for shipping gold and silver and a key slave-trading port. Bogotá was founded in 1538. The region became the centre of the Viceroyalty of New Granada.
Communities of escaped Africans, such as San Basilio de Palenque, maintained their independence and culture.

history.heading: Independence and the 19th century
paragraphs: Independence was declared in 1810 and secured by Simón Bolívar's victory at the Battle of Boyacá in 1819. The country formed part of Gran Colombia with Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama until 1830. Panama separated in 1903 with US support.
Liberals and Conservatives fought repeated civil wars, including the Thousand Days' War (1899–1902).

history.heading: La Violencia, conflict and peace
paragraphs: The assassination of Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948 triggered La Violencia, a decade of partisan violence that killed around 200,000 people. In the 1960s guerrilla groups such as the FARC and ELN emerged, later followed by right-wing paramilitaries. Drug cartels, such as Pablo Escobar's Medellín cartel, became extremely powerful in the 1980s and 1990s.

The conflict killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. A peace agreement with the FARC was signed in 2016, earning President Juan Manuel Santos the Nobel Peace Prize, though violence by other armed groups continues. In 2022 Gustavo Petro became Colombia's first left-wing president.

culture.heading: A diverse nation
paragraphs: Colombia's population is mainly mestizo, with large Afro-Colombian communities, especially on the Pacific and Caribbean coasts, and more than 80 indigenous peoples. Spanish is the official language, and dozens of indigenous and creole languages are recognised. Most Colombians are Catholic.
Gabriel García Márquez, author of One Hundred Years of Solitude and Nobel laureate, made magical realism famous. Fernando Botero is known for his voluminous figures.

culture.heading: Music and festivals
paragraphs: Colombia is famous for music: cumbia and vallenato from the Caribbean coast, salsa from Cali, and global stars such as Shakira, Carlos Vives, J Balvin and Karol G. The Barranquilla Carnival is one of the largest in the world and recognised by UNESCO.
Food includes bandeja paisa, arepas, ajiaco soup and sancocho, and Colombia is famous for its coffee. Football and cycling are hugely popular; Egan Bernal won the Tour de France in 2019.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Colombia is a unitary presidential republic. The president is elected for a single four-year term. Congress has a Senate and a House of Representatives. Colombia has one of the longest traditions of electoral democracy in Latin America, despite decades of armed conflict.
Key political issues include implementing the peace process, dealing with remaining armed groups and drug trafficking, rural development, inequality and reforms to health and pensions.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Colombia has historically been one of the closest US allies in Latin America, cooperating on drug policy. It has hosted nearly three million Venezuelan migrants. It is a member of the Pacific Alliance and the Andean Community and the only Latin American global partner of NATO.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Colombia has one of the largest economies in Latin America. Oil and coal are the main exports, followed by coffee, flowers (Colombia is the world's second-largest flower exporter), bananas, gold and emeralds.
Manufacturing, services and tourism have grown strongly since the peace agreement. The currency is the Colombian peso.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Colombia has high income inequality, a large informal sector and regional disparities. Illegal coca cultivation, of which Colombia is the world's largest producer, fuels violence. The government aims to move away from fossil fuels toward renewables and tourism.
